evidence: Cic. Tusc. 1.43: caelum hoc, in quō nūbēs, imbrēs, ventīque cōguntur
terms.comment: The sky, and the weather in it (serēnum caelum, a clear sky; see clear sky); caelum suspicere, to look up at the sky. The plural caelī, the heavens, is poetic and Church Latin (Lewis & Short).

phrases.english: What if the sky fell in right now? (said of a needless fear)

phrases.latin: prōnaque cum spectent animālia cētera terram, ōs hominī sublīme dedit, caelumque vidēre jussit et ērēctōs ad sīdera tollere vultūs
phrases.english: while the other animals look down at the ground, he gave man an upturned face, and bade him look at the sky and lift his eyes to the stars

phrases.latin: Crepusculō caelum prīmum rubēbat, tum violāceum fīēbat, postrēmō nigrum
phrases.english: At dusk the sky was red at first, then turned violet, and at last black
phrases.source: Libellus VI, Reditus: per Alpēs domum

sources: John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, p. 136.
Terence and Cicero checked against the Latin Library text (CLTK mirror); Ovid from the Latinitas loci collection (loci-ovidius).
Theodōrus et pater · Ad Larem avītum, Libellī I–VII, as they stood on 9 November 2026. Examples marked “Libellus” quote those texts word for word.
